The important implication of Theorem 2.4 is that there is no crossing term in the splitting matrix, unlike the standard Hessian matrix. Therefore, the splitting effect of an individual neuron only depends on its own splitting matrix and can be evaluated individually; the splitting effects of different neurons can be compared using their splitting indexes, allowing us to decide the best subset of neurons to split when a maximum number constraint is imposed. As shown in Algorithm 1 , we decide a maximum number m ∗ m_{*} of neurons to split at each iteration, and a threshold λ ∗ ≤ 0 \lambda_{*}\leq 0 of splitting index, and split the neurons whose splitting indexes are ranked in top m ∗ m_{*} and smaller than λ ∗ \lambda_{*} .

The computational cost of exactly evaluating all the splitting indexes and gradients on a data instance is 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ d 3 ) \mathcal{O}(nd^{3}) , where n n is the number of neurons and d d is the number of the parameters of each neuron. Note that this is much better than evaluating the Hessian matrix, which costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 3 ) \mathcal{O}(N^{3}) , where N N is the total number of parameters (e.g., N ≥ n ​ d N\geq nd ). In practice, d d is not excessively large or can be controlled by identifying a subset of important neurons to split. Further computational speedup can be obtained by using efficient gradient-based large scale eigen-computation methods, which we investigate in future work.

Note that our splitting matrix (see Eq. 7 ) involves the second order information of the activation function. In practice, we replace all ReLu activation with Softplus to prevent numerical issues in calculating the splitting matrices. We also apply this in other following experiments that contain ReLu activation function in the network.

new_distinct_scoped_primary_papers.conclusion: Direct prior for balanced-copy perturbations, common-vs-contrast second-order decomposition, residual-weighted neuron/logit-curvature matrix and negative-eigenvector splitting. Prior applies loss after averaging neuron outputs; current continuation has mean own-member CE and adds PSD spread curvature. Current graph-band first-order VJP directions do not select splitting curvature.

In contrast, we propose end-to-end training of GBDT and GNN called BGNN (for Boost-GNN). As before, we first apply GBDT and then GNN, but now we optimize both of them taking into account the quality of final predictions. The training of BGNN is shown in Figure 1 . Recall that already built decision trees cannot be properly tuned due to their discrete structure, so we iteratively update GBDT model by adding new trees such that they approximate GNN loss function.

In Algorithm 1 we present the training of BGNN model that combines GBDT and GNN for any node-level prediction problem such as semi-supervised node regression or classification. In the first iteration, we build a GBDT model f 1 ​ ( 𝐱 ) f^{1}(\mathbf{x}) with k k decision trees by minimizing the loss function L ​ ( f 1 ​ ( 𝐱 ) , y ) L(f^{1}(\mathbf{x}),y) averaged over the train nodes, following equation ( 2 ). Using all predictions f 1 ​ ( 𝐗 ) f^{1}(\mathbf{X}) , we update the node features to 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime} that we pass to GNN. Possible update functions that we experiment with include concatenation with the original node features and their replacement by f 1 ​ ( 𝐗 ) f^{1}(\mathbf{X}) .

Next, we train a graph neural network g θ g_{\theta} on a graph G G with node features 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime} for all nodes by minimizing L ⁡ ( g θ ​ ( G , 𝐗 ′ ) , Y ) L(g_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}),Y) with l l steps of gradient descent. Importantly, we optimize both the parameters θ \theta of GNN and the node features 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime} . Then, we use the difference between the optimized node features 𝐗 n ​ e ​ w ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{new} and the input node features 𝐗 ′ = f 1 ​ ( 𝐗 ) \mathbf{X}^{\prime}=f^{1}(\mathbf{X}) as the target for the next decision trees built by GBDT. If l = 1 l=1 , the difference 𝐗 n ​ e ​ w ′ − 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{new}-\mathbf{X}^{\prime} exactly equals the negative gradient of the loss function w.r.t. the input features 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime} multiplied by the learning rate η \eta :

𝐗 n ​ e ​ w ′ = 𝐗 ′ − η ​ ∂ L ⁡ ( g θ ​ ( G , 𝐗 ′ ) , Y ) ∂ 𝐗 ′ . \mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{new}=\mathbf{X}^{\prime}-\eta\frac{\partial L(g_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}),Y)}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{\prime}}\,.

In the second iteration, we train a new GBDT model f 2 f^{2} , with the original input features 𝐗 \mathbf{X} but new target labels: 𝐗 n ​ e ​ w ′ − 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{new}-\mathbf{X}^{\prime} . Intuitively, f 2 f^{2} fits the direction that would improve GNN prediction based on the first predictions f 1 ​ ( 𝐗 ) f^{1}(\mathbf{X}) . In other words, GBDT approximates the gradient steps made by GNN for the node features 𝐗 \mathbf{X} .

After f 2 f^{2} is trained, we combine the predictions f ⁡ ( 𝐗 ) = f 1 ​ ( 𝐗 ) + f 2 ​ ( 𝐗 ) f(\mathbf{X})=f^{1}(\mathbf{X})+f^{2}(\mathbf{X}) and pass the obtained values to GNN as node features. GNN model g θ g_{\theta} again does l l steps of backpropagation and passes the new difference 𝐗 n ​ e ​ w ′ − 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{new}-\mathbf{X}^{\prime} as a target to the next iteration of GBDT. In total, the model is trained for N N epochs and outputs a GBDT model f : 𝐗 ↦ Y f:\mathbf{X}\mapsto Y and GNN model g θ : ( G , 𝐗 ) ↦ Y g_{\theta}:(G,\mathbf{X})\mapsto Y , which can be used for downstream tasks.

Intuitively, BGNN model consists of two consecutive blocks, GBDT and GNN, which are trained end-to-end, and therefore can be interpreted from two angles: GBDT as an embedding layer for GNN or GNN as a parametric loss function for GBDT. In the former case, GBDT transforms the original input features 𝐗 \mathbf{X} to new node features 𝐗 ′ \mathbf{X}^{\prime} which are then passed to GNN. In the latter case, one can see BGNN as a standard gradient boosted training where GNN acts as a complex loss function that depends on the graph topology.

new_distinct_scoped_primary_papers.conclusion: Primary Section3/Algorithm1 establishes repeated fitting of new additive trees to graph-GNN input-feature updates. For one inner step this target is the negative graph-dependent prediction-loss gradient. It is different from fixed masked logit-residual spectral bands and copied private-factor route initialization. No Hessian selector or mean-zero private route expansion is specified in these inspected passages; not a full-paper absence claim.

Then, we determine the scaling factor ζ \zeta according to Theorem 3.2 to ensure rank and scale stability. Thus, based on Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 , we propose a novel initialization method, LoRA-GA. By hooking into PyTorch’s backward process, we compute the gradient for one layer at a time and discard the computed gradients immediately. This ensures that our memory usage remains at O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) instead of O ⁡ ( L ) O(L) , where L L is the number of layers. This approach allows the memory consumption during the initialization phase to be less than that during the subsequent LoRA finetuning phase. Our algorithm is shown in Algorithm 1 . If the sampled batch size is large, we can also use gradient accumulation to save memory further, as shown in Algorithm 2 .

passages.text: 2.2 Repulsive force in function space

To overcome the aforementioned overparameterization issue, the update in Eq. ( 3 ) can be formulated in function space instead of weight space. Let 𝒇 : 𝐰 ↦ f ⁡ ( ⋅ , 𝐰 ) {\bm{f}}:\mathbf{w}\mapsto f(\cdot\,;\mathbf{w}) be the map that maps a configuration of weights 𝐰 ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} to the corresponding neural network regression function and denote 𝒇 i := f ⁡ ( ⋅ , 𝐰 i ) {\bm{f}}_{i}:=f(\cdot\,;\mathbf{w}_{i}) the function with a certain configuration of weights 𝐰 i \mathbf{w}_{i} . We can now consider n n particles in function space { 𝒇 i } i = 1 n \{{\bm{f}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} with 𝒇 ∈ ℱ {\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F} and model their interaction with a general positive definite kernel k ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) k(\cdot,\cdot) . We also consider the implicit functional likelihood p ⁡ ( 𝒚 | 𝒙 , 𝒇 ) p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{f}}) , determined by the measure p ⁡ ( 𝒚 | 𝒙 , 𝐰 ) p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}},\mathbf{w}) in the weight space, as well as the functional prior p ⁡ ( 𝒇 ) p({\bm{f}}) , which can either be defined separately (e.g., using a GP) or modeled as a push-forward measure of the weight-space prior p ⁡ ( 𝐰 ) p(\mathbf{w}) . Together, they determine the posterior in function space p ⁡ ( 𝒇 | 𝒟 ) p({\bm{f}}|\mathcal{D}) . The functional evolution of a particle can then be written as:

𝒇 i t + 1 \displaystyle{\bm{f}}_{i}^{t+1} ← 𝒇 i t + ϵ t ​ ϕ ​ ( 𝒇 i t ) \displaystyle\leftarrow{\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}+\epsilon_{t}\phi({\bm{f}}_{i}^{t})\, with ϕ ⁡ ( 𝒇 i t ) \displaystyle\text{with}\qquad\phi({\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}) = ∇ 𝒇 i t ​ log ​ p ​ ( 𝒇 i t | 𝒟 ) − ℛ ⁡ ( { ∇ 𝒇 i t k ​ ( 𝒇 i t , 𝒇 j t ) } j = 1 n ) . \displaystyle=\nabla_{{\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}}\log p({\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}|\mathcal{D})-\mathcal{R}\left(\left\{\nabla_{{\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}}k({\bm{f}}_{i}^{t},{\bm{f}}_{j}^{t})\right\}_{j=1}^{n}\right)\,. (4)

However, computing the update in function space is neither tractable nor practical, which is why two additional considerations are needed. The first one regards the infinite dimensionality of function space, which we circumvent using a canonical projection into a subspace:

For any A ⊂ 𝒳 A\subset\mathcal{X} , let π A : ℝ 𝒳 → ℝ A \pi_{A}:\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{X}}\to\mathbb{R}^{A} denote the canonical projection onto A A , that is, π A ​ ( f ) = { f ⁡ ( a ) } a ∈ A \pi_{A}(f)=\{f(a)\}_{a\in A} .

In other words, the kernel will not be evaluated directly in function space, but on the projection k ⁡ ( π B ​ ( f ) , π B ​ ( f ′ ) ) k\big(\pi_{B}(f),\pi_{B}(f^{\prime})\big) , with B B being a subset of the input space given by a batch of training datapoints. The second consideration is to project this update back into the parameter space and evolve a set of particles there, because ultimately we are interested in representing the functions by parametrized neural networks. For this purpose, we can use the Jacobian of the i i -th particle as a projector:

ϕ ⁡ ( 𝐰 i t ) = ( ∂ 𝒇 i t ∂ 𝐰 i t ) ⊤ ​ [ ∇ 𝒇 i t ​ log ​ p ​ ( 𝒇 i t | 𝒟 ) − ℛ ⁡ ( { ∇ 𝒇 i t k ​ ( π B ​ ( 𝒇 i t ) , π B ​ ( 𝒇 j t ) ) } j = 1 n ) ] . \phi(\mathbf{w}_{i}^{t})=\left(\frac{\partial{\bm{f}}^{t}_{i}}{\partial\mathbf{w}^{t}_{i}}\right)^{\top}\left[\nabla_{{\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}}\log p({\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}|\mathcal{D})-\mathcal{R}\left(\left\{\nabla_{{\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}}k(\pi_{B}({\bm{f}}_{i}^{t}),\pi_{B}({\bm{f}}_{j}^{t}))\right\}_{j=1}^{n}\right)\right]\,. (5)

cached_primary_evidence_reused.conclusion: Jacobian-transpose projection of output-space cotangents into ensemble parameter updates is prior. No exact equivalence to the complete fixed graph initializer is asserted.
